BRYONY GORDON: The brave women who helped convict Russell Brand have allowed me to acknowledge the truth about my own experiences with him when I was 25

I was 25 when I was sent to interview Russell Brand. He was an up-and-coming comedian and had just begun presenting a Big Brother spin-off show, and despite what his lawyer Ian Winter KC said in court, I had no idea of his reputation, other than that he was a few years clean and sober from heroin addiction. We met in a cafe in Primrose Hill, and I remember being completely thrown when this funny, sparky Fagin-like creature almost immediately began propositioning me, telling me how beautiful I was and asking if he could kiss me. I remember I giggled a lot. Afterwards, he insisted on walking me to the Tube station, and the whole way there, he continued to ask if he could kiss me, while I continued to tell him he couldn't. I returned to the office, and within moments my phone began ringing - he had got my number from his PR. And so began a bombardment, 20 or 30 phone calls and texts a day.

Send an amphibious force 300 miles across the ocean to seize a poorly defended archipelago known only to penguin enthusiasts and whalers. My mum lived with dementia for 8 years. My adult son & I shared the responsibility. Even when nursing home care becomes inevitable your job is not done. You still have to supervise, advocate for them, negotiate with the care home as well as managing their financial affairs, sell the family home, keep accounts for the Office of the Public Guardian. But I never found the information hard to get & I don't think, for me, a support network would have helped. It wouldn't have stopped the heartbreak, or the exhaustion of coping with the demands alongside a full time job. It wouldn't have stopped me walking the beach in the rain so I could cry freely & the tears wouldn't show as I watched her decline. It wouldn't have stopped me having to sell my vintage (because I'm vintage) childhood teddy to help meet the care costs the government won't help with. The information & support is there already. It's the heartbreak & exhaustion that gets you.
